title: Screen Directors Playhouse: Spellbound
text:
Constance Peterson & Dr. Murchison

“Your work is brilliant but lifeless… There is no intuition in it.” —Dr. Murchison
Constance rebuffs Murchison’s attempts to “improve” her as both a doctor and woman. Their discussion ends as she leaves to meet the new chief of staff.

title: Screen Directors Playhouse: Spellbound
text:
Arrival of “Dr. Edwards”
Constance meets the supposed Dr. Anthony Edwards, newly appointed to Green Manors.
A moment of tension arises when Edwards draws lines with his fork on a white tablecloth—triggering an odd reaction.

title: Screen Directors Playhouse: Spellbound
text:
The Garms Patient
A patient, Garms, insists:

“I killed my father.”

Edwards becomes fascinated with the case, but later collapses during an emergency.

title: Screen Directors Playhouse: Spellbound
text:
First Romantic Tension
That night, Constance confronts Edwards about her feelings.

“Something has happened to us… It happens in a moment sometimes.” —Edwards

But mid-embrace, he recoils at the sight of her white robe with dark lines, shuddering.
Soon after, Garms attempts suicide.

title: Screen Directors Playhouse: Spellbound
text:
Empire State Hotel
Constance finds him registered as John Brown (J.B.).
She insists on helping him recover his memory.
He remembers:

A cigarette case with initials J.B.
A sudden headache upon seeing it

Nothing before arriving at Green Manors

Constance pushes him:

“Your guilt is imagined. It comes from childhood.”

But he argues logically that he must have been with Edwards when he died.

title: Screen Directors Playhouse: Spellbound
text:
Newspaper Break
A headline appears:
“Police Hunt Dr. Constance Peterson — Believed Aiding Madman”
They flee to Rochester to visit Dr. Brulov, Constance’s mentor.

title: Screen Directors Playhouse: Spellbound
text:
The Color White
The white bedspread terrifies J.B.
Constance forces him to look at it:

“White… dark lines…”

He clutches a straight razor without knowing why.
He suddenly flashes an image:

“An old man… the razor…”

But the memory collapses.

title: Tasks Remaining
text:
Targeted messages, that are based on our online activities and the extensive algorithms, is the tax of this internet/AI era.
For a while, these recommendations were saturated with travel ideas. Probably due to my searches and patterns on Google Maps and YouTube watching, as well as more general internet search history.
While I usually resist these digital offerings, one caught my eye: “Nine Cities You Must Visit in Your Lifetime.”
I was surprised by what I found.
Of the nine global destinations, I had already visited seven. Only Istanbul and Cape Town remained on the list.
I had visited those 7 cities during a 4-year assignment in Korea, either as part of a business trip or due to work compensation package that became a family vacation.

During that expatriate period in the pre-Internet era, I was the beneficiary of a world that felt limitless.
Overseas travel, upgraded hotel accommodations, and fine dining were not just perks; they were the environment I lived in.
I grew accustomed to the visibility and the rewards, and in my youthful state, I simply expected that trajectory to continue indefinitely.
However, the “return” proved to be its own kind of mission. Upon arriving back at my point of origin, the visibility vanished and the compensation packages stayed behind. My life returned to the quiet rhythm I had known before the assignment. The transition was jarring; the readjustment to a “normal” life took a long time to navigate, and even longer to fully accept.
Now, in this stage of my life, I am faced with a different kind of task. I am reminded of the words of the physicist Erwin Schrödinger:
“The task is… not so much to see what no one has yet seen; but to think what nobody has yet thought, about that which everybody sees.”
When I was a “corporate warrior,” my travel was easily justified. It was funded by business needs and corporate strategy. But now that the armor is off and the company-sponsored journeys have ended, the challenge has changed.
How do I prioritize and balance my lingering desire to travel—to see what I “have yet seen”—with this new mandate to think “what nobody has thought” about the everyday world? How do I find the extraordinary within the ordinary, normal setting of my daily life?

Perhaps this is the ultimate “return.” After years of seeking the “new” across seven cities and multiple continents, I am learning that the most profound discoveries don’t require a passport or a corporate compensation package. They require a change of heart and a sharpening of the mind.
As a corporate warrior, I was a collector of sights. Today, I aim to be a cultivator of insights. It is a quieter, more humble task—to sit in the “everyday” and find the eternal truths that others might walk right past. Whether I am standing at a quiet graveside in Sanpete County or watching the next generation of my family establish their own orbits, I am finally beginning to see.
I no longer need the euphoria of a new destination to escape reality. Instead, I am choosing to stay right here, thinking what nobody has yet thought about that which everybody sees. In the end, the most “precious” (귀한) journey isn’t the 100 kilometers into the mountains or the flight across the Pacific—it is the short, sacred distance from the eye to the heart.

title: Precious Returns
text:
Learning a foreign language after the teenage years is an exercise in humility.
It is a struggle.
Same challenge is faced by those trying to reclaim a “mother tongue” that was either never fully learned or long forgotten.
One of the hurdles is the “near-miss”—words that sound almost identical but carry vastly different, even contrasting, meanings.
My son, who served a mission in the western islands of 日本, recalls a time he was teaching about God sending His kind and gentle son to earth.
He intended to use the word 温厚 (Onkou), but in the heat of the moment, a similar-sounding word slipped out with a totally different meaning. Fortunately, the gravity of his message and the listener’s tolerance for a “rookie” mistake saved the discussion.
I can relate. Even with a native tutor (my wife) for over thirty years, I still struggle with the subtle nuances of Korean and the weight of Chinese-character-based words (한자, 漢字).
I used to wonder why missionaries were considered so “valuable” upon their return.
In Korean, the word for “Return” is 귀환 (Gwihuan), 返回, 帰還, while the word for “Precious” or “Valuable” is 귀한 (Gwihan), 貴重 or 寶貴的.
Perhaps the value of the returnee isn’t just in the work they did, but in the “precious” perspective they gained while struggling to distinguish subtle differences in language.
But in doing so, conquering the small nuances can bring about bigger changes or bridge those languages and cultural differences.


The power of these two words became real to me recently when we set out to find the missionaries who taught and baptized Sister K’s family over forty years ago.
While we had maintained a lifelong friendship with Elder A—even attending his homecoming from a Mission Presidency—we had lost contact with Elder B decades ago.
Thanks to the persistent efforts of Sister K’s sister and her husband, we finally located him.
We traveled 100 kilometers into Sanpete County, arriving at a small town near a temple dedicated in 1888.
I was given a difficult task: approach the door and introduce our family to a man I had never met, bridging a four-decade gap in a single conversation.
Standing on his doorstep, I felt like a new missionary back in CLAM (California Los Angeles Mission). Awkwardly began to recount the story of Sister K’s conversion. At first, there was only the blank surprise of a stranger. But slowly, the veil of time lifted. His memory returned, his face transformed, and he invited me in.
Sister K joined us shortly after, and for ninety minutes, the room was filled with the spirit of the early Church in Korea.
We relived the days of the pioneers—the members and elders who shaped the foundations of our faith. We especially enjoyed his stories of teaching English to Korean businessmen, those same men whose donations eventually allowed the New Horizon and Tender Apples groups to perform in Daejeon.
In that living room in Sanpete County, the distance between Utah and Korea, and the four decades between us, nearly vanished.


During my early days with the Korean Branch, some of the members used to tease me. Because my Korean was so lacking, they would joke:

“Surely you must be 화교 (Overseas Chinese)!”

I took the teasing in stride and persevered. Over time, I became as proficient in the language as any 귀환 선교사 (returned missionary). But more than just language, my understanding of the gospel and my love for the people of 나성 (Los Angeles) deepened into something permanent.
Moreover, I developed a foundation for life that has served me well: A Korean person, living in the United States, belonging to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. In that intersection of identities, a root was firmly planted.
I feel a deep gratitude for the missionaries who sacrificed so much to work among the Korean people—especially those who served in the 1960s and 70s, when living conditions were far from easy. Those missionaries didn’t just teach us a new religion; they taught us our universal roots within the gospel.
Because of their efforts, we were given the chance to dream big within the “gospel tent.” Many of us have since realized the very dreams our parents first set forth for us. This journey has helped me realize anew that missionaries are both 귀한 (precious) and 귀환 (returned).
They are precious for what they gave, and they are returned to us to remain as lifelong brothers and sisters.
I can now clearly envision a grand reunion—not just in a small town in Sanpete County or in megapolis that is 서울, but a heavenly one—where missionaries are welcomed home and rewarded by the generations of those they taught and influenced.

title: Old Familiar Song
text:
As we prepared for the congregational hymn, the choir director—visible and striking in her Christmas-red outfit—stood to lead us. Her enthusiasm and love were unmistakable, radiating through the choir and out into the pews. I am certain the congregation felt that same warmth, though I couldn’t see their faces; I was facing forward, which was fortuitous, as I had begun to cry.
In that moment, I was transported back in time to 3790 MD-410, on the East-West Highway in Hyattsville—the place I called my spiritual home for nine years.
I vividly remembered that same spirit in Sister L. and the others who led us in songs so long ago.
My heart began to soften, and my spirit lifted.
It felt as though the veil had thinned, and perhaps the angels and those who have passed on had descended just enough to join their voices with ours.


We are known as the United States of America, but perhaps we would be better described as the United Communities or United Families of America.
When I first joined that congregation fifty-one years ago, we possessed virtually nothing in the way of physical belongings. We had a budding spiritual understanding, but we lacked established family traditions—especially for the Christian celebration of Christmas.
Everything we learned and experienced was church-centered and supported by our “Ward Family.” We immersed ourselves in Christmas devotionals, and I still vividly remember a powerful message regarding the importance of a father’s involvement. Later, I watched with pride as my own father participated, playing the role of one of the Three Wisemen.
We gathered in the homes of other families to learn Christmas carols and to observe, for the first time, what a true holiday gathering looked like. I took note and expressed gratitude internally, hoping to practice those traditions so I could carry them forward into my own life.


The messages and the music were terrific. Every year I find myself saying the same thing:

“It simply cannot get any better than this.”

But it does.
How is it possible for a gathering of only three hundred individuals to produce a performance of this caliber? Even with minimal practice, the result matched the beauty and professional standard required to invite the Spirit.
As the Bishop mentioned, our Ward has undergone significant demographic changes; we are now, officially, a “top-heavy” ward.
There was a time when certain families in our midst could have fielded an entire string ensemble on their own.
Today, while the internal talent pool may not be as vast as it once was, it has become more refined—-augmented beautifully by the presence of friends and visitors.
It was a gentle and a sweet reminder that a nation is sustained by a union of communities, and those communities are built upon a foundation of dedicated families.
We gather not just to celebrate, but to learn and practice the mandates of life—striving, year after year, to move a bit closer to the ideals of our faith.
It is through practicing these ideals that my heart is opened.
By exercising the very concepts that make a community thrive, we help our country excel.
In this land, we prove that the old familiar story can be or should be, and so it has changed:

There is a room in the Inn—the one we call America.

title: With Wondering Awe
text:
Wondering Awe

“With Wondering Awe” is a Christmas carol unique to the Latter-day Saint hymnal; but it is not of Latter-day Saint origin, and its author and composer have remained a mystery. The current hymnal indicates both words and music are anonymous, from Laudis Corona, a Catholic collection published at Boston in 1885.

Excerpt from [With Wondering Awe, Latter-day Saint Hymnology] (https://ldshymnology.wordpress.com/2018/12/23/with-wondering-awe/)
1.
With wond’ring awe the wisemen saw The star in heaven springing, And with delight, in peaceful night, They heard the angels singing:
Hosanna, hosanna, hosanna to his name!
2.
By light of star they traveled far To seek the lowly manger, A humble bed wherein was laid The wondrous little Stranger.
Hosanna, hosanna, hosanna to his name!
3.
And still is found, the world around, The old and hallowed story, And still is sung in ev’ry tongue The angels’ song of glory:
Hosanna, hosanna, hosanna to his name!
4.
The heav’nly star its rays afar On ev’ry land is throwing, And shall not cease till holy peace In all the earth is growing.
Hosanna, hosanna, hosanna to his name!

title: Mother of Pearls
text:
My parents purchased a matched set of storage cabinets—bedroom and living room—beautifully crafted, with 1960s mother-of-pearl inlays.
Technically, the 찬장 was meant for the kitchen.

But in my parents’ home, it became the centerpiece of the living room.
When they moved west—2,100 miles (3,400 km)—those cabinets came with them. They made the journey just as faithfully as my parents’ hopes and fears.
It wasn’t that my parents were unaware of trends.

They saw friends upgrade to bigger houses in newer neighborhoods.

They watched their children move into modern homes with modern decor.
Yet they held onto these familiar, outdated cabinets.

Hopelessly out of style… and yet irreplaceable.
Now that Sister K lives in the home, we sometimes wonder whether we should let them go. Sell the furniture. Start fresh. Move out of the past.
But neither of us can.

Not yet.
To discard them feels like discarding a part of our parents—a piece of their immigrant journey, their sacrifices, their hopes for something better. Those cabinets hold more than clothes and keepsakes; they hold the echoes of a life built through effort, persistence, and faith.
So, for now, we will keep them.

Maybe for a long time.
They are the last, tangible link to the memories and spirit of our ever-seeking, ever-striving parents—and we’re not ready to let that go.

title: Recorded Memories
text:
My uncle, born in 1943, is the last remaining member of that generation in our family.
I recently sent him a family video—a collection of old photos set to music, capturing moments from my immediate family over the years. When I called him on a popular social networking service, he told me he had received the message and watched the video.
We talked about the health of our older relatives and the progress of his three grandchildren, who are now finishing school and entering the workforce. He also shared that he had undergone three surgeries to remove cancerous growths. It is remarkable that modern medicine has given him so many additional years.
I asked if he remembered a moment from long ago, when our family won a radio contest. Before television became widespread, radio was the center of daily life. My uncle had submitted the names of everyone in the family, and on the day of the announcement, we all gathered around the radio to listen.
The announcer said:
“인천시… 남구… 주안동… 246번지.”
Everyone grew excited.
Then he called my name.
My uncle threw me into the air in celebration. We traveled together to Seoul to claim the prize. But after deducting service fees and taxes, the reward had shrunk to the price of lunch for two.
I told my uncle this story again during our call. He didn’t remember it.
If something doesn’t touch your life directly, it fades from memory.



Growing up, I often heard my father tell the story of how his family escaped from North Korea.
His maternal uncle had walked most of the 100-plus miles from Seoul to 안변, 함경도 to find them and bring them south.
[Link to Uncle 김동훈 finding the family, https://oakhi.github.io/Life-Begins-When/posts/20230103%2038th%20Parallel/index.html]
After arriving in South Korea, my father found work at a Japanese furniture company. When Japan surrendered at the end of World War II and its officials left, my father assumed responsibility for one of the manager’s homes.
He was only fifteen years and five months old at the time.

My uncle had a slightly different version of events.
He remembers his mother saying he was about one year old when the family left North Korea for Seoul. That would place their departure around 1944.
This raises questions: would that have given my father enough time to get established, earn the trust of local workers, and eventually occupy a house that once belonged to a company manager?
What we do know is that my father’s maternal uncle played a key role in guiding the family out of the North. We also know that my father worked for a Japanese furniture company, and that our family lived in that house well into the Korean War and even afterward.
What we don’t know is when exactly the maternal uncle arrived in North Korea to help them, or the precise moment the family left their home and resettled in Seoul.
I have no reason to believe my father or my uncle shared anything untrue. Rather, I believe both of their recollections are correct—pieces of a story that likely unfolded across several stages.
It is entirely possible that my father’s family traveled south in multiple groups: perhaps my grandfather and the older children left first to get established, followed by another group with younger siblings, and finally the youngest children and my grandmother.
This pattern would not be unusual. When we ourselves moved to United States, my father went a month ahead to prepare things. And when we returned to Korea years later for an expatriate assignment, I left in January, with Sister K and the children following about two months later.
Instead of trying to force a single “official” version of the story—based on memories that naturally differ—I hope to capture our family history simply as it was told by those who lived it. Where dates or details are missing, I will record what is known and allow readers to imagine the rest.
My hope is that these memories serve as a reminder of how the God of Israel has guided our family—through war, through hardship, and into a new world filled with hope.

title: Labels and Classifications

Koreans have long engaged in various forms of fortune telling—사주 (Saju), 무당 (Mudang) traditions, and 풍수 (Pungsu). Elements of 무당 even show up in modern pop culture; the recent K-Pop Demon Hunters movie, though made for younger audiences, drew on storylines instantly recognizable to older Koreans who grew up around these beliefs.
Yet practices like these are best viewed as cultural heritage—entertainment, not instruction. Their real value, perhaps, lies in reminding us that life can be shaped and reshaped, rather than rigidly defined by the year, month, day, and hour of one’s birth.
I’m certain my mother never followed 사주. And even if others had charted out a destiny for me, she would have insisted that I follow her vision of my future—one grounded in purpose, faith, and what God intended for my life.
Thank you, Mother, for instilling that belief.

title: Neighborhood Mart
text:
It felt at first like stepping into the lobby of a small, old-world hotel—quiet, warm, and softened by music drifting from the southwest corner.
The source wasn’t a sleek sound bar or Bluetooth speaker, but a sturdy white box from an earlier era—the kind Steve Jobs might have unveiled onstage. Yet from it came something unmistakably timeless.
If you listened with just a bit of imagination, you could almost hear Autumn Leaves by Johnny Mercer floating through the room:

The falling leaves drift by the window, The autumn leaves of red and gold…


And in this space, the melody felt perfectly at home.
Like Goodwood Park Hotel.






The room carried a gentle nostalgia—simple tables, soft natural light, and the faint aroma of simmering broths or pan-seared dishes lingering from the kitchen. It echoed the familiar charm of eateries tucked away in East Asian side streets:
서울 · 東京 · 臺北 · 香港
Places where the food is honest, the hospitality understated, and the atmosphere unpretentious enough that you relax without thinking about it.
Sometimes we go searching for places like these—seeking flavors, sounds, and textures from faraway cities. Other times, if we’re patient, those places come to us instead, quietly settling into our own neighborhoods, waiting to be noticed.
This spot is one of them.

Familiar yet foreign, modest yet comforting, it rewards anyone willing to step inside, take a seat, and let the experience unfold.
If you find yourself nearby with a quiet moment to spare, stop in—some places reveal their charm only when you sit down and stay awhile.
Let Hana Mart carry you back to the quiet side streets you remember, and the ones your heart still hopes to visit.
Be sure to say 안녕하세요 to Sister K, aka, Mama June.

A Faithful Neighbor
Two dozen grandchildren gathered and sang “I Am Trying to Be Like Jesus.”

Among them, a boy—about eight or nine years old—was overcome with emotion, tears covering his face throughout the song.

He was thinking of his grandfather, who had recently passed away—just thirteen days after learning of his cancer diagnosis.


—


A Neighbor and a Friend
He was my neighbor—his home sat just west of the road we shared.
We had been neighbors for 23 years.

He was born twenty years before me, and he had married at the same age as I did.

He and his wife raised eight children—twice as many as Sister K and I.

One time, while I was searching for a new role, I came across a position in the Captstone Program he had developed. I sent him my résumé, asking if he thought the role might be a good fit.

He sent two replies: the first, expressing doubt; the second, after reviewing again, saying he had changed his mind and believed I would be a good fit.

That was him—always encouraging, always believing in others.



An Example of Quiet Service
On the west side of our home stands a tree that once grew too fast for its own good. I decided to trim it, though I lacked experience.

A heavy branch fell in an unexpected way, bending the metal fence below. I assumed it couldn’t be fixed and moved on.
Later, my neighbor noticed it. Without ever mentioning it to me, he found a way to reshape the fence back to its original form.

He did this quietly, while another family was renting that house. I only learned about it later—an act of quiet service, done without recognition.



A Christlike Legacy
During the funeral, three of his children spoke, each offering a glimpse into a home where discipleship was lived daily.

They described a father who took a brief detour to a hardware store—on the way to the hospital where his daughter was about to give birth.

They spoke of mornings that began with scripture study and family prayer, and even monthly personal priesthood interviews.

He kept a binder to track each child’s progress, concerns, and goals—a loving steward of his family’s spiritual growth.
After his diagnosis, he shared this message, the last public one :

“I am grateful that Heavenly Father trusted me to have this experience, so that I can learn further what Christ went through.”

His longtime colleague2 and neighbor—former dean of BYU Law School—paid tribute by describing him through the lens of the Boy Scout Law 3:

A Scout is trustworthy, loyal, helpful, friendly, courteous, kind, obedient, cheerful, thrifty, brave, clean, and reverent.

He embodied each of these.



A Farewell in Faith
As the funeral procession left the chapel, five Model A Fords followed the limousine—cars just like the ones he loved to restore.

One story told how, at age twelve, he bought his first Model A from a butcher at a grocery store. It became a lifelong passion, symbolic of his knack for rebuilding and restoring—not just cars, but people and relationships.
Thank you, Brother Bob, for all you have done and all you have quietly taught.

Showing a glimpse of what celestial life would be. Building up a family in love, learning about and working on all things pertaining to the kingdom.

text:
Finding out or having a better understanding of the complexity of the temporal world around us does not diminish its mysteries or meaning in our lives.
Seasons in the northern hemisphere and its attendant changing colors or foliage.
Creation of a new person and followed by a 9 month gestation period, and a miraculous birth and the sacrifice of the mother.
Death of individuals are individualist yet all appointed to close this chapter in the eternal journey.

The Four season cycle seems eternal when young.
As one matures, the lessons are given and received
And the finite nature of our lives are understood and accepted.
However, in the eternal sense, the cycles of season does repeat and we will be renewed.

Autumn has a peculiar stillness that invites reflection. The air cools and sharpens, carrying the faint sweetness of decay — the scent of leaves surrendering their color to time. Light, once bright and commanding, grows tender and slanted, as if aware of its own diminishing. Shadows stretch longer, and the days seem to exhale.
In these quiet transformations, we sense something profoundly human. The trees do not resist their fading; they release with grace. Their surrender is not defeat but fulfillment — the completion of a cycle written into their being. Watching them, we are reminded that our own lives, too, must learn to let go — of seasons, of people, of selves we once were.
The four-season cycle seems eternal when we are young. Each spring returns as if nothing had changed, and time feels circular, generous, and unending. But as one matures, the lessons are given and received; the rhythm that once seemed endless reveals its deeper truth. We begin to understand, and even accept, the finite nature of our own lives.
Yet in the eternal sense, the cycles of the seasons do repeat — and through them, we are promised renewal. The falling leaf is not an end, but a pause before the quiet work of winter and the green return of spring.
Whether it is the season of the year or the period of life, the fall (秋) is most melancholy season of all.
Particularly this year, there seems to be many deaths.
Don’t know if there are more deaths in one season versus another.
Even so, the death seems more poignant during the fall season

title: Korean Congregations
text:
Everywhere Korean people congregate there seems to be,
Korean run, for Korean businesses.
The minimal number to support such set up is small.
The other ever present element are Churches set up for Koreans.
Often they start by utilizing or sharing a space with existing churches.
Then they outgrow and purchase or build their own churches.
This is repeated wherever Koreans immigrate to.
This pattern was repeated and enlarged in the Los Angeles area.

Wherever Korean communities take root abroad, two institutions seem to appear almost without fail: Korean-run businesses and Korean churches.

The number of people required to sustain these is surprisingly small. A few families, a handful of entrepreneurs, and soon a network forms — a grocery store, a restaurant, a beauty salon, a travel agency.
Alongside these enterprises, churches arise as the spiritual and social heart of the community.

Often they begin humbly, sharing space with an existing congregation, renting a hall on Sunday afternoons.

But as the congregation grows, so does its ambition: they purchase land, construct buildings, and establish permanent institutions.
This pattern seems to repeat itself wherever Koreans have immigrated — based on my experiences of living in Washington DC area and from spending time at a sprawling metropolitan area in Southern California.

Nowhere is this more visible than in Los Angeles, where the concentration of Korean churches has made religion not only a matter of faith but also a marker of ethnic presence and solidarity.

“I will be your father”, Dallin Oak’s maternal grandfather upon his father’s death

title: A Memorial Service
text:
A difficult set of questions arose before the event.
Due to a sudden traffic accident, we found ourselves preparing a service of remembrance.
Just two months earlier, during our visit to Korea, she shared with us her future plans to re-visit her home country and her love for painting.
Those attending would be primarily ethnic Koreans—mostly first-generation immigrants and their children.
Many of the older attendees would prefer a Korean-language service, while the younger generation, less fluent in Korean, would be unable to follow. After thoughtful discussion, it was decided that the service would be conducted in English, so the younger family members could participate more fully.
The greater challenge was in determining the nature of the service—how it should be framed, and which customs or traditions to follow. Should it take on a religious form or remain secular?
For those that live in Utah, such matters seldom arose and discussed openly. Lack of contact from ecclesiastical representatives suggested her recent absence from the congregational activity.
This left her husband and three sons with the responsibility of planning the service. I was invited to officiate, at a ceremony to be held 1,400 miles away in a lakeside city.
As we boarded the plane, we received the finalized program. It followed the tradition of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (예수 그리스도 후기 성도 교회), the faith community she and her family had attended during the years we knew them.


Seventeen days passed between her unexpected passing and the funeral. During that time, the family devoted themselves to honoring, remembering, and loving their wife, mother, and grandmother. In the absence of a single overriding tradition, they chose instead a universal approach to saying farewell to a mortal life.
They remembered her fierce determination, tenacity, and hard work—her deep appreciation for education and knowledge. Late in life, she had studied painting and took joy in creating family portraits. The night of her passing, she had been working on a portrait of her third son.
They honored her by recalling her teachings and wisdom. She possessed a remarkable intellect; had she been born in this modern era, she might have become a medical doctor. Instead, she raised three sons who each pursued professions in dentistry and medicine.
As they recounted her life, I thought of my own shortcomings and limitations. As I often do, I quietly pledged to be a better person, husband, and father.
The family expressed their hope and assurance in reunion in the life to come.

As the autumn midday cast its intermittent light through drifting clouds, she was laid to rest in a site chosen by the family–a final resting place until her resurrection, when body and spirit are reunited.
As services ended and family members said their goodbyes, I recalled words she had spoken years earlier, during the Holladay period, when I was dating Sister K.

Don’t see her as she now is, working in a menial, physical job to support her education. She is from a good family.

She was saying in essence,

But rather, see her as she truly is, and as she was and is to become

Her words echoed a Christian belief that we had a noble beginning and that we are here to prove ourselves to be worthy of our eternal life.
That we all

…are taken home to that God who gave them life. (Alma 40:11)

Thank you 황이모 for your life, your example, and your enduring love.

갑작스러운 교통사고로 인해, 우리는 추모 예배를 준비하게 되었습니다.
불과 두 달 전, 한국을 방문했을 때 그녀는 고국을 다시 찾고 싶다는 계획과 그림에 대한 사랑을 우리에게 이야기했습니다.
참석자 대부분은 한인 1세대 이민자와 그 자녀들이었습니다.
연로한 참석자들은 한국어 예배를 선호했지만, 젊은 세대는 한국어에 익숙하지 않아 내용을 따라가기 어려웠습니다. 깊은 논의 끝에, 젊은 가족 구성원들이 더 온전히 참여할 수 있도록 예배를 영어로 진행하기로 결정되었습니다.
더 큰 고민은 예배의 성격이었습니다. 어떤 형식으로 해야 하는가, 어떤 전통을 따라야 하는가. 종교적 의식을 따를 것인가, 아니면 세속적인 추모로 할 것인가.
유타에 사는 이들에게 이런 문제는 거의 논의된 적이 없었습니다. 교회 대표자들의 연락이 없었던 것으로 보아, 최근에는 교회 활동에 참여하지 않았던 것으로 보였습니다.
결국 남편과 세 아들이 예배를 준비해야 했습니다. 나는 가족의 초청으로, 1,400마일 떨어진 호숫가 도시에서 집례를 맡게 되었습니다.
비행기에 오르기전에, 완성된 예배 순서지를 받았습니다. 그것은 그녀와 가족이 우리가 알던 시절 함께 다녔던 예수 그리스도 후기 성도 교회(The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) 의 양식을 따르고 있었습니다.
그녀의 갑작스러운 별세로부터 장례식까지 열일곱 날이 흘렀습니다. 그 기간 동안 가족은 한결같은 마음으로 아내이자 어머니, 할머니였던 그녀를 기리고, 추억하며, 사랑했습니다.
하나의 절대적인 전통 대신, 그들은 인간의 삶을 떠나보내는 보편적 방식을 택했습니다.
그들은 그녀의 강인한 의지와 끈기, 그리고 부지런함을 기억했습니다. 배움과 지식에 대한 깊은 존중을 지녔던 그녀는 인생의 후반기에 그림을 공부하며 가족의 초상화를 그리는 즐거움을 누렸습니다. 그녀가 세상을 떠나던 그날 밤에도, 셋째 아들의 초상화를 그리고 있었습니다.
가족은 그녀의 가르침과 지혜를 떠올리며 그녀를 기렸습니다. 그녀는 비범한 지성을 가진 분이었습니다. 만약 지금의 시대에 태어났다면, 아마도 의사가 되었을 것입니다. 대신, 그녀는 치의학과 의학의 길을 걸은 세 아들을 길렀습니다.
그녀의 삶을 되새기며, 나는 나 자신의 부족함과 한계를 떠올렸습니다. 그리고 언제나 그랬듯이, 속으로 더 나은 사람이자 남편, 아버지가 되겠다고 다짐했습니다.
가족은 다가올 세상에서의 재회를 향한 희망과 확신을 나누었습니다.
가을의 한낮, 흩어지는 구름 사이로 비치는 햇살 속에서, 그녀는 가족이 선택한 묘지에 안장되었습니다. 그것은 부활의 날, 몸과 영혼이 다시 하나 되는 그날까지의 마지막 안식처였습니다.
예배가 끝나고 가족이 마지막 인사를 나누는 동안, 나는 오래전 할러데이 시절 그녀가 내게 했던 말을 떠올렸습니다.
“그녀를 지금의 모습으로만 보지 마세요. 학비를 벌기 위해 육체적인 일을 하는 모습으로만 보지 마세요. 그녀는 좋은 가정에서 자란 사람입니다.”
그녀가 진심으로 말하고자 했던 뜻은 이러했습니다.
“그녀가 진정 어떤 사람인지, 그리고 어떤 사람이었고 또 어떤 사람이 될 사람인지를 보세요.”
그녀의 말은 우리 모두가 고귀한 시작을 지녔으며, 이 생에서 우리의 영원한 생명에 합당함을 증명해야 한다는 기독교 신앙의 핵심을 울려주었습니다.
우리 모두는 결국

title: Phyllis’ Musical Inn
text:
When I travel, I expect to meet people.
Whether I’m meeting new people or crossing paths with an old friend.
Because I live in a small town, our new, four-gate airport acts as a reliable social hub; I know that making a friendly encounter is a high probability event — much like trip to the local supermarket.
This experience is much different at the metropolis to our north.
That city, is a sprawling enclave with nearly ten times our population, funnels its air traffic through a massive 71-gate airport.
While our small airport concentrates human flow, their colossal facility disperses it, turning the simple act of recognizing someone in the crowd from an expectation into a statistical long shot.
Took the requisite 1/4 mile (1735 ft or 530 meters) hike to the gate near the western end of Terminal A.
I found myself dwelling on the cost of this last-minute trip. I ended up paying nearly the same as a trans-Pacific flight just to travel 1,250 miles to the third-most-populous metropolitan area in the United States.
Then I saw a face I recognized, but I couldn’t remember when and where we worked together.
Took the risk of being wrong and introduced myself. At that moment, I remembered when and where.
2008 to 2010 at NOC.
He tells me nearly everyone that worked there are millionaires, but not necessarily multimillionaires.1
We shared the notes on who we remember from those days. Jim B, Mike C, and Neal D.
He said he retired at my current age.
Tried to commit him to a role, but he was being evasive.
He didn’t want to be associate with the “smart” group.2
He decided to go see his son play in a band.
A last minute decision that will set him back well over $1000.3
His son was playing at the Phyllis’ Musical Inn on 1800 West Division Street.
Thought about joining him but we are here for a funeral and will have an early start.
Thought about retirement and our impromptu decisions.
Would I book a last minute flight to see a family member perform.
He stopped working early and is enjoying life.
I was glad that he recognized me and we were able to visit about the NOC days.
I need to reevaluate my priorities.
I have known a number of individuals with advanced degrees.
Then there are those that I have worked with, like Dan, that I didn’t know had advanced degrees.
They were just a normal, easy to get along person that got things done at work.
It seems to me there are 2 groups of people with PhDs.
Ones that announce and wants you to know their standing and understanding.
The second group takes more slow approach.
Letting others discover their understanding of the subject matter and slowly establish their standing.
Thanks Dan, for reminding me about setting priorities and letting the world catch up to you instead of the other way around.
Also, for maintaining your style so that I can recognize you in a crowd.

title: Level Up
text:
Koreans help one another during celebrations and in times of sorrow.
부조금(扶助金) or assistance money is given and received to help ease the burden of wedding celebration or to allay or cover funeral expenses.
When my mother passed away, Dad’s youngest brother, who lived with us until he was married, about 12 years, sent a large sum of money as 부조금(扶助金).
When we called to thank him and asked why so much. He said, to repay his debt to her, he should have sent a lot more.
His reasoning was then my mom, elevated his life’s standing, or raised his level in the society by educating him.
This was at a time when per capita income was couple hundred dollars.

The education arrangement was that, as long as the uncle passed entrance exams, my mom would support him financially.
We have a common saying, “Kangs are good at taking exams” Instead of saying we are good students. I suppose one can’t be one without the foundation.
One time, money was really tight. Mom asked the uncle to take time off and serve in the military. She told him, perhaps by the time he completes his service, things will be better.
This was a time when there was no military draft in Korea. Thus, to volunteer for the military service was an admission of a dire situation. My uncle recognizing the severity of the situation, volunteered.
My earliest memory is visiting him with mother. He was stationed near Pusan, in a place called 김해. It must have taken mom and a better part of a day to travel 400 to 500 km in those days.

That uncle graduated and was married. Though he was youngest, he took care of grandma for over 30 years, after we left Korea. As well as taking care of matters that were normally handled by the oldest son. So my uncle obtained education but he also paid off the tuition by providing much needed service to the family.
Nearly 60 years after my mom housed him and educated him, his words were one of gratitude.

Mothers in those days must have had a special talent. They made us feel that we were not poor but we were blessed and had a great potential to succeed. And amazingly we all believed we could achieved anything and we were not that poor as statistics would later suggest.

I still unsure how she did it. But here is my guess.
My mother determined that her children would not go through what she went through. War caused famine and lost opportunity for education. We would eat high quality food and earn education, even if it meant my parents sacrificing their comfort.

So my uncle is correct. We all benefitted from my mother’s sacrifice. We are all elevated or live a higher level life because of her.

Mahler’s 2nd Symphony: Resurrection in the 21st Century
Gustav Mahler’s Symphony No. 2, the “Resurrection,” stands as one of the most profound musical meditations on life, death, and the hope of transcendence. Composed in the late 19th century, it reflects Mahler’s own confrontation with mortality and spiritual longing. Yet more than a historical artifact, the symphony resonates powerfully in the 21st century, a world defined by rapid change, existential uncertainty, and the search for meaning.
Mahler’s era was one of societal tension and personal anxiety. The late Romantic period fostered grand artistic expression, yet Mahler’s life was marked by illness, loss, and the awareness of his own mortality. The Resurrection Symphony embodies this consciousness through its expansive five-movement structure. From the dramatic opening of the first movement, which confronts death directly, to the final choral adagio that envisions a spiritual awakening, the symphony charts a journey from despair to transcendence. Mahler’s orchestration—massive, intricate, and emotionally charged—invites listeners into an intimate yet universal experience, bridging personal grief and collective hope.
At the core of the symphony is a philosophical engagement with human existence. The first movement begins with somber motifs that evoke mortality, while the slow second movement offers introspection and lament. The vigorous scherzo of the third movement provides contrast, reflecting human resilience and vitality. Mahler then transforms the music in the fourth movement, introducing a contemplative, almost otherworldly quality through orchestral color and vocal text. The final movement, employing a full chorus and soloists, sets Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock’s poetry to music, declaring the triumph of the spirit over death—a vision of resurrection that is both personal and communal.
Historically, the symphony challenged its early audiences with its scale and spiritual ambition, yet it influenced generations of composers, from Schoenberg to Shostakovich, and became a staple of concert repertoire. Today, its relevance extends beyond the concert hall. In the 21st century, Mahler’s exploration of mortality resonates amid global crises, pandemics, and climate change. The symphony’s trajectory—from despair to hope—mirrors the collective human need to confront uncertainty and find meaning, offering a form of emotional and spiritual catharsis.
Furthermore, Mahler’s integration of orchestral, choral, and textual elements anticipates contemporary multimedia approaches to art and performance. Modern productions often incorporate visual and technological enhancements, underscoring the symphony’s timeless capacity to engage audiences across disciplines. Its universal themes transcend culture and geography, uniting listeners in reflection, empathy, and communal experience—a reminder that music remains a powerful medium for shared human understanding.
In conclusion, Mahler’s Symphony No. 2 is far more than a monumental Romantic work; it is a living, breathing exploration of life’s ultimate questions. Its capacity to confront death, celebrate resilience, and imagine transcendence ensures its continued relevance. In an era marked by uncertainty, the Resurrection Symphony offers a musical framework for hope, collective reflection, and the enduring human spirit.

American stop-motion animated fantasy film
Kubo and the Two Strings is a stop-motion animated fantasy steeped in Japanese folklore and myth. The film follows Kubo, a boy who can animate origami with music from his shamisen (a three-stringed instrument). He lives quietly, caring for his ill mother, until supernatural forces—his mother’s sisters and his grandfather, the Moon King—hunt him down.
To survive, Kubo embarks on a quest to find three magical items that once belonged to his father, a fallen samurai. Along the way, he is guided by Monkey and Beetle, companions who embody loyalty, sacrifice, and forgotten family ties.
The journey is both external and deeply personal: Kubo confronts loss, memory, and the stories that shape identity. Ultimately, instead of defeating his grandfather through violence, Kubo redefines the conflict through compassion and storytelling—transforming vengeance into remembrance and forgiveness.

American animated fantasy comedy-drama film
Coco (2017, Pixar/Disney) is an animated film set in Mexico that explores themes of family, memory, and cultural tradition through the lens of the Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead).
The story follows Miguel, a 12-year-old boy who dreams of becoming a musician despite his family’s long-standing ban on music. When he secretly borrows a guitar from a shrine to his idol, the late singer Ernesto de la Cruz, he is magically transported to the Land of the Dead.
There, Miguel meets his ancestors and discovers family secrets—most importantly that de la Cruz is not the hero he seemed, and that his true great-great-grandfather is Héctor, a forgotten musician struggling to be remembered.
The film emphasizes that remembering and honoring loved ones keeps them alive in spirit, while being forgotten is a “final death.” By the end, Miguel reconciles his passion for music with his family’s values, restoring harmony between generations.

Memory & Storytelling: Coco focuses on remembering loved ones to keep them alive in spirit, while Kubo portrays storytelling as a weapon against oblivion, a way to transform grief into meaning.
Mortality & Loss: Both tackle death openly, but in different tones. Coco is tender, celebratory, and hopeful. Kubo is darker and melancholic, blending the inevitability of loss with the possibility of emotional survival.




Cultural Lens

Coco draws from Mexican traditions like Día de los Muertos, presenting a vibrant, colorful afterlife where joy and remembrance sustain family bonds.
Kubo takes inspiration from Japanese folklore and Buddhist ideas, with themes of impermanence, ancestral spirits, and transformation.

Coco is musical, lively, and emotionally warm—its message is broadly accessible and uplifting.
Kubo is poetic, visually striking, and more contemplative, often leaning toward the somber beauty of myth.

Together, these films show two cultural perspectives on the universal human experiences of loss, memory, and family. Coco comforts us with the idea that love transcends death when we remember, while Kubo challenges us to face mortality with courage, compassion, and the transformative power of storytelling.

Sunzi Bingfa (孫子兵法, Art of War) – by Sun Tzu (pre-Han, ~5th century BCE)

Wu Zi (吳子) – by Wu Qi (Warring States general).

Emphasized discipline, logistics, and civil-military relations.

Wei Liaozi (尉繚子) – a Qin/Han text.

Tai Gong’s Six Secret Teachings (太公六韜, Liutao) – attributed to Jiang Ziya (Zhou strategist).

Focus on civil and military balance, leadership, and moral authority in warfare.


👉 These, along with other texts, were later collected into the Seven Military Classics (武經七書) (canonized in the Song dynasty), but the Han dynasty already circulated and studied them.

Book of Documents (尚書, Shangshu)

Ancient collection of speeches and edicts; used in the Han as a Confucian classic for legitimizing rule.

Records of the Grand Historian (史記, Shiji) – by Sima Qian (c. 94 BCE)

Official dynastic history; detailed accounts of institutions, law, economy, and military campaigns.

Huang-Lao Texts (黃老學) – blending Daoism, Legalism, and pragmatism.

Great question. Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) is not just a chronology—it’s a literary and philosophical work that weaves together history, biography, morality, and political thought. Here are the major themes scholars usually highlight:


1. The Mandate of Heaven & Cyclical History


Dynasties rise and fall because of virtue (de) or the loss of it.

Heaven grants or withdraws legitimacy depending on rulers’ morality and ability.

Shiji illustrates this cycle through narratives of Xia, Shang, Zhou, Qin, and Han.





2. Human Agency vs. Fate


Tension between individual choices and forces beyond control.

Figures like Xiang Yu (the failed conqueror) show the tragedy of brilliance undone by circumstance.

Sima Qian suggests that fate sets limits, but human judgment and character still matter.





3. Morality, Virtue, and Exemplars


History as moral instruction: good rulers uphold ritual, benevolence, and justice; bad rulers indulge in cruelty and excess.

Biographies highlight models (Confucius, ministers of Zhou) and warnings (tyrannical Qin Shi Huang, corrupt officials).





4. The Role of Officials and Advisors


Emphasis on the importance of wise ministers and loyal remonstrators.

Many biographies of courtiers, generals, and strategists stress loyalty, courage, or betrayal.

A warning that rulers who ignore good advice invite ruin.





5. The Ordinary and the Marginalized


Sima Qian breaks ground by including merchants, assassins, wandering knights, astrologers, jesters, etc.

These stories show that history is not only about kings but also about those at society’s edges.





6. Heroism and Tragedy


Admiration for bold individuals who challenge fate, even if they fail.

The tragic arcs of figures like Jing Ke (the would-be assassin of the Qin king) or Qu Yuan (the poet-statesman) highlight human dignity amid defeat.





7. Memory and Legacy


Sima Qian stresses the importance of recording deeds for posterity, even when the person failed in life.

His own preface, written after his disgrace and castration, underscores the theme: history gives people lasting voice beyond shame or death.





8. Integration of Myth, History, and Philosophy


The Shiji blends legendary origins (Yellow Emperor, Yao, Shun) with verifiable historical records.

It is both a Confucian moral history and an effort to preserve cultural memory as a unified narrative.



✅ In sum:

The Shiji is about the rise and fall of power, the tension between virtue and ambition, and the human struggle against fate. It’s simultaneously a political manual, a collection of moral biographies, and a deeply personal meditation on history and memory.

The Records of the Grand Historian (史記 Shǐjì) is one of the most important works in Chinese history and literature. Here’s an overview in plain, interview-style language:



What It Is


Written by Sima Qian (司馬遷), a court historian during the Han Dynasty (around 91 BCE).

It is the first comprehensive history of China, covering more than 2,000 years—from the legendary Yellow Emperor (~2600 BCE) through the reign of Emperor Wu of Han.

Contains 130 chapters, blending history, biography, philosophy, and storytelling.





Structure
The work is divided into five sections:


Basic Annals (本紀 Běnjì) – Chronicles of emperors and ruling houses.

Chronological Tables (年表 Niánbiǎo) – Timelines to keep events across states and dynasties aligned.

Treatises (書 Shū) – Thematic essays on subjects like music, economics, law, astronomy, and rituals.

Hereditary Houses (世家 Shìjiā) – Histories of feudal lords and major noble families.

Biographies (列傳 Lièzhuàn) – Lives of notable figures—officials, generals, scholars, foreign peoples, even assassins and merchants.





Why It Matters


Foundation of Chinese Historiography: Established the model for later dynastic histories (正史 Zhèngshǐ).

Literary Value: Written with vivid, often dramatic storytelling; sometimes reads like a novel.

Balanced Perspective: Sima Qian included both emperors and commoners, victors and rebels—unusual for ancient histories.

Moral Voice: Shows his Confucian values but also independence; Sima Qian himself suffered disgrace and castration yet still completed it, turning personal tragedy into a monumental legacy.





Influence


Considered the “father of Chinese history.”

Influenced later historians such as Ban Gu (Book of Han), and even Chinese prose style in general.

Still read today in China and worldwide for insights into leadership, politics, culture, and human character.



👉 In short: The Records of the Grand Historian is a sweeping, 2,000-year account of China’s past, written with literary flair and historical rigor, setting the standard for all future Chinese history writing.

Accuracy in Academia (AIA)’s founder, Reed Irvine, died November 16, 2004 at the age of 82. Born in 1922, he served his country in World War II as a marine. He really never stopped serving his country.
He started Accuracy in Media (AIM), AIA’s parent organization, in 1969, to scrutinize the then-dominant old media at a time when few questioned its reporting. From the time he retired as a Federal Reserve Board economist in the 1970s until late last year, when he suffered a serious heart attack, he worked for AIM full-time.
It is fair to say that the so-called new media—Fox News, talk radio and even internet blogs—that prove the reporting of the venerable CBS News and company to be inaccurate are rushing through a door that Reed Irvine opened when he started going head-to-head with media heavyweights such as then-Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee.
Reed Irvine started AIA in 1985 because he saw that too many professors were using classrooms the way that too many reporters used newsrooms—to influence events rather than provide actual accounts of the past and present. He served as chairman of AIA until his death.
Since the 1980s, his standards have guided AIA. In his late seventies, he went toe to toe with demonstrators who attempted to disrupt an AIA conference at Columbia University in New York City.
When I first came to AIA last year, I read an e-mail that Reed forwarded around the office. He answered one of AIM’s critics by writing, “Show me one thing that we have written that is inaccurate.” No one could.
On October 22, 1985, Izvestiya, the state-run newspaper in the then-still existent Soviet Union, ran an article on the founding of Accuracy in Academia (AIA). Of all of the press coverage that AIA has received in its history, the Izvestiya write-up is arguably the most historically significant. Entitled ‘The Hunt For Freethinkers,’ the piece took aim at the then-infant group’s purpose.
“By the look of things, henceforth students, with the start of their activities, will take out fountain pens and tape recorders,” Izvestiya predicted. “Teachers at universities are quivering with fear,” the Soviet press organ reported. “They tremble at the utterance of each word.”
“For who knows?,” Izvestiya asked rhetorically. “Are the students taking notes on their lectures for their own purposes, or are they listening for the purpose of reporting what the teacher says to the ultra-right organization, Accuracy in Academia?”
Izvestiya normally confined itself to attacking U. S. government policies and American society in general. Leveling a front-page broadside at a small non-profit group represented somewhat of an editorial departure for the journal. The attention Izvestiya devoted to AIA, then, gave the watchdog group quite a distinction.
“The reactionary newspaper, The Washington Times, crows over the report that Accuracy in Academia, which has only existed for a few days, already has gathered voluntary informants on 110 university campuses throughout the United States,” Izvestiya noted.
“At the call of their spiritual mentor, worshippers and apprentices of McCarthy hunt for teachers who have the courage to adhere to liberal convictions,” according to Izvestiya. The McCarthy that Izvestiya refers to is the late Sen. Joseph R. McCarthy, R-WI, famous for his investigations of communists in U. S. government jobs.
“By such measures, these teachers are labeled ‘Marxists,’ which in contemporary America is pregnant with the most serious consequences,” Izvestiya asserted. “For example, political science professor Bertell Ollman knows this from personal experience for he dared admit that he was actually on the side of Marxism. Solely because of that he was not allowed to compete to fill a position at the University of Maryland.”
Six years after the Izvestiya article appeared, the Soviet Union itself imploded and the Cold War ended. This year, AIA celebrates 19 years of life and is still in business. Visited a place where food was fit for Goldilocks.
It wasn’t too spicy, too salty, but just right.
While there, took many photos, some came out better than I expected.
In fact, all of them were technically just right, as algorithm dictated it to be.
Didn’t have to make any travel plans.
Hosts took care of it, I just had to be ready and they chauffeured me from places to places using the latest navigation tools.

During the visit, I didn’t get lost – while we were with locals.
Consequently, I never learned how to figure out directions or where I was visiting.
By looking at metadata on photos, I could retrace places I visited.
In the days past, I would be asking directions even after planning with physical maps.
Looking for landmarks, such as banks or natural indicators that provides directional anchors.
Also studying the sun’s position aided in determining the direction in the absence of landmarks such as mountains.
This approach was mistake-prone but after a day or so, one usually figured out the lay of the land.






Figure 1: 창덕궁, near 37°34’45.4”N 126°59’32.4”E




One rainy afternoon, I ventured out on my own.
Initial thinking was that I could locate palaces, since most landmarks remained same in that part of town.
I miscalculated.
My assistant was the locally made, on-line map, which had details often lacking multi-purpose maps made outside the country.
However, since I couldn’t figure out my current location, the e-Maps were not as helpful.
To figure out the immediate location, I had to move about, which was difficult to notice on a small phone screen.
Finally resorted to asking people where I needed to go.
Some were friendly and some were helpful, some were neither.
At last, tried the strategy of following tourists to the tourist destination.






Figure 2: Within 비원



Food was not only presented well and flavored ideally, but also there were over abundance of it.
Growing up, food was scarce and meals were served plain.
We mostly ate vegetables, fishes and occasional meat-enhanced soups.
Food was local and seldom got to taste cuisine from other locations
We tasted meat, a couple times a year, usually during holidays or birthdays of older people.
On this trip, we got to sample food from all regions of the country, while in the capital city.
Special occasion food was available on-demand, all hours of the day.
One could eat food from days gone by as well as order food that was from other countries.
At a wedding banquet, the buffet line featured 5 separate offerings.
A line of traditional Korean food, followed by seafood selection, fruit and salad, and dessert.
An hour and half allotted time was not enough to sample all the food and to visit with relatives.^[in the wedding venues, scheduled are tightly set and each couple has 30 to 40 minutes to use the main hall and guests are directed to the dining hall afterwards, before the next couple starts their cycle of activities]
Chose to visit with relatives, for some it was nearly 30 years since we last saw them.






Figure 3: Closer to Food from earlier years



The society had transformed from scarcity and inconvenient mode to one of utmost abundance and comfort.
During 50 years, the pace of growth and transformation has been remarkable.
Kudos to the people of Korea their achievements that borders on miracle.
As an observer of the change, it seemed that in days of past, one was faced with daily challenges and inconvenience.
Lack of food and walk to nearly all places.
In the present day, there are more food than the population 2 or 3 times can consume.
In addition, one has to look for ways to exercise, to find a way to walk to places and and try to get lost and try the personal navigation skills rather than rely on electronic help.

Not to suggest that those days were preferable to present day.
Days of poverty, hunger and physical demands
But in some ways, discomfort, pain and hardship allowed for and provided comparison and appreciation.
And perhaps a slow build up of character.
Is there a way to accomplish it, during these Goldilocks days?

text:
Key Characteristics of 한국가곡:
Lyrics in Korean
Unlike Western lieder (like Schubert or Schumann), Korean art songs are sung in standard Korean, often using poetry by modern Korean poets or texts that evoke traditional Korean values and imagery.
Western Musical Form
The structure, harmony, and vocal techniques are borrowed from Western classical music, particularly the German lied and French mélodie traditions.
Emphasis on Emotion (정서, jeong-seo)
Themes often revolve around longing, nature, love, nostalgia, and han (한) — the uniquely Korean feeling of deep sorrow or unresolved grief.
Piano Accompaniment
Most Korean art songs are composed for a solo voice with piano, similar to Western art songs.
Performance Tradition

These songs are frequently performed in recitals, competitions, and school curriculums for vocal students in Korea.

Refined Narrative: The Korean Mission and the Cultural Divide
My mother’s kindness made our family one of the beneficiaries of the services provided by early missionaries in the Land of the Morning Calm. I remember Elder R serving in Seoul (서울), Daejeon (대전), and Incheon (인천) between 1976 and 1978. He was one of an estimated 1,650 to 3,000 missionaries who served during the first three decades of the Church’s efforts there.
These young men—mostly from the United States, predominantly Idaho or Utah, with an occasional missionary from places like New Mexico or Australia—faced real dangers, including the ever-present threat of 연탄가스중독 (carbon monoxide poisoning) from the coal briquettes used for heating.
They often told us that while the Church might seem like a foreign, “wilderness” faith outside the Korean mainstream, it was considered entirely mainstream back home in the States.
That assertion felt confusing when we moved to the Eastern U.S., just three years after our baptism. In Maryland, we were once again members of a church that felt distinctly outside the mainstream. It wasn’t until I relocated to Provo, Utah, fifteen years later, that the young missionaries’ words finally clicked into place.
In Utah, I understood their perspective entirely. The Church was not just a religion; it was the entire social landscape. The neighborhood was the congregation, and the surrounding culture was the community. Here, I witnessed a unique and sometimes jarring blend of church and state seldom seen elsewhere, realizing that the missionaries’ concept of “mainstream” was entirely defined by their specific cultural enclave.

title: A Temporary Life in Korea
text:
Physical and Economic Hardship (1950s–1960s)
The immediate post-war environment presented extreme physical challenges, particularly for the first groups of missionaries who arrived in the mid-1950s.

Poverty and Reconstruction: South Korea was severely underdeveloped and impoverished.2 Missionaries lived in conditions far removed from Western middle-class standards, often lacking reliable electricity, running water, and modern sanitation.
Infrastructure: Travel was difficult and slow due to damaged or rudimentary infrastructure. This complicated the logistics of mission operations, from securing supplies to coordinating with the sparse number of local members across the country.
Disease and Health: Exposure to unfamiliar diseases and the generally poor public health environment posed significant risks.
Language Barrier (Initial Phase): The first missionaries had to navigate daily life and teach with extremely limited access to resources for learning Korean (Hangul).3 While the LDS Church later developed formalized language training, early efforts were often based on local, on-the-ground learning. The Book of Mormon was not published in Korean until 1967, which was a major limitation in their teaching materials for the first decade.4

title: A Temporary Life in Korea
text:
Cultural and Social Challenges (1960s–1980s)
Missionaries encountered a society deeply rooted in Confucianism and Buddhism, which made conversion difficult due to fundamental differences in lifestyle and social structure.5

Confucianism and Family Structure: The strong emphasis on filial piety and ancestral worship (Jesa) in Korean Confucian culture was the greatest hurdle. Joining the LDS Church often meant rejecting or modifying these deeply held family practices, leading to severe social and familial persecution for new Korean converts. Missionaries struggled to help converts balance their new faith with their respect for parents and ancestors.
Competition with Traditional Christianity: Korea already had a strong presence of Protestant denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian) that had been established since the late 19th century. LDS missionaries had to distinguish their message from existing Christian groups, which sometimes viewed the LDS Church with suspicion or criticism.
Military Presence and Association: In the earliest years, the Church’s presence was largely built upon the efforts of U.S. Latter-day Saint servicemen stationed in Korea.6 While this provided a foundation, it also initially linked the Church to the American military presence, potentially hindering its acceptance as an independent, universal faith among some segments of the Korean population.

title: A Temporary Life in Korea
text:
Political Environment and Security
The constant political instability and threat of conflict created a tense atmosphere for foreigners.

Post-War Instability: The decade following the armistice was characterized by political volatility, anti-communist sentiment, and occasional civil unrest. While missionaries generally avoided political involvement, the unstable environment posed a constant security concern.
Travel Restrictions: During periods of high tension or government limitations, the ability of missionaries to travel freely within the country and secure visas was often challenging. The government had to officially recognize the Church before formal missionary efforts could commence and be sustained.7

1. Steps to Donate Assets


Form the Foundation


Incorporate as a nonprofit corporation in your state (usually via Secretary of State).

Adopt bylaws and appoint a board of directors.

Apply for IRS recognition of tax-exempt status (Form 1023).



Transfer Ownership of Assets


Automobiles: Title must be transferred to the foundation’s name at the DMV.

Office equipment (computers, furniture, printers): Use a Bill of Sale or Donation Agreement transferring ownership to the foundation.

Keep detailed records (serial numbers, VINs, condition reports).



Value the Assets


Cars: Use IRS fair market value guides (Kelley Blue Book, Edmunds) to determine donation value.

Equipment: Appraisal or fair market estimate (Craigslist/eBay comps, or a professional appraisal if large).

Required: IRS Form 8283 (Noncash Charitable Contributions) if the donation is over $500; appraisal required if over $5,000.



Record the Contribution


Foundation records the donation as an in-kind contribution at fair market value.

Donor receives a donation receipt issued by the foundation.



IRS Filing


Donor claims the deduction on Schedule A (Form 1040).

Foundation records the contribution on its annual Form 990-PF.

title: Notes

2. Benefits for the Donor
✅ Immediate Charitable Deduction


Donor can deduct the fair market value of the assets (subject to IRS limits — usually up to 30% of AGI for private foundation gifts).


✅ Avoid Capital Gains Tax


If the asset has appreciated (e.g., office equipment purchased cheaply but still valuable), donor avoids capital gains by donating instead of selling.


✅ Control Over Philanthropy


Unlike giving directly to a public charity, donating to your own foundation allows you (and family/board) to decide how funds and assets are used.


✅ Legacy Building


The foundation becomes a permanent vehicle for charitable giving in your family’s or business’s name.

Public Charity vs. Private Foundation
Great question! Here’s a clear breakdown of the difference between a Public Charity and a Private Foundation under IRS §501(c)(3):

title: Notes
text:
1. Common Ground
Both Public Charities and Private Foundations are nonprofit organizations recognized by the IRS under 501(c)(3). That means they are:


Tax-exempt on income related to their charitable purpose.

Eligible to receive tax-deductible donations.

Organized for purposes like religion, education, scientific research, arts, or relief of the poor.

title: Notes
text:
2. Public Charity
Definition:


A public charity is a 501(c)(3) that receives broad public support (from many donors, government grants, or program revenue).


Key Features:


Funding source: Must get a significant portion of income (at least 1/3 in many cases) from the general public, other charities, or government.

Examples: Churches, schools, hospitals, universities, museums, food banks.

Control: Usually governed by a diverse board, not a small group or family.

IRS Oversight: Generally lighter than private foundations.

Donor Tax Deduction: Donors can deduct up to 60% of AGI (adjusted gross income) for cash gifts.

title: Notes
text:
3. Private Foundation
Definition:


A private foundation is a 501(c)(3) that usually has a single major funding source (like a family, individual, or corporation).


Key Features:


Funding source: Funded primarily by one person, family, or company, not broad public support.

Examples: Gates Foundation, Ford Foundation, family foundations.

Control: Often run by its founders, family members, or a small group.

IRS Oversight: Heavier reporting and operating restrictions.

Payout Requirement: Must distribute at least 5% of assets annually for charitable purposes.

Excise Tax: Pays a small excise tax on investment income.

Donor Tax Deduction: Donors can deduct up to 30% of AGI for cash gifts.

Would you like me to also explain how the IRS decides whether a new nonprofit is classified as a public charity or private foundation by default (hint: new 501(c)(3)s are usually private foundations unless they qualify for public charity status)?
Perfect — let’s go into how the IRS actually classifies a new 501(c)(3) organization at the start:

title: Notes
text:
Default Rule


When you apply for IRS 501(c)(3) recognition (Form 1023), the IRS by default classifies you as a Private Foundation.

Why? Because it’s easier to assume one person/family is funding you until you prove otherwise.

title: Notes
section: How to Qualify as a Public Charity
text:
How to Qualify as a Public Charity
To be recognized as a Public Charity instead of a Private Foundation, you must meet one of the following tests:

1. Institutional Public Charities (Automatic Public Charity)
Some organizations are always considered public charities, regardless of funding:


Churches, synagogues, temples, mosques

Schools, colleges, universities

Hospitals and medical research organizations

Governmental units (when acting for charitable purposes)





2. Public Support Test
For most other nonprofits, the IRS checks whether you have broad public support:


One-Third Support Test:

At least 33⅓% of your total support must come from the public (individuals, government grants, other charities).

Facts and Circumstances Test (10% Test):

If you get at least 10% public support and can show you are actively seeking broad support (fundraising, grants, memberships), you may still qualify as a public charity.





3. Supporting Organizations
Some nonprofits qualify as supporting organizations if they are organized and operated exclusively to support one or more existing public charities (e.g., a “friends of the library” group).

title: Notes
section: What Happens if You Don’t Qualify?
text:
What Happens if You Don’t Qualify?


If you can’t show enough public support → the IRS will classify you as a Private Foundation.

But: You can later convert to public charity status if your donor base broadens.

title: Notes
text:
Key Takeaway


All new 501(c)(3)s start as private foundations by default.

To be a public charity, you must either:


Be in an automatically qualified category (church, school, hospital, etc.), OR

Pass the public support test (show enough donors/grants).

title: Bonus Life
text:
When my grandmother Kim (김옥돌) was born, the life expectancy for Koreans was 25 to 35 years — largely because of high infant mortality.
Yet she lived to be 92, outlasting that estimate by nearly sixty years.
When my parents were born in the 1930s, life expectancy had risen only slightly — 32.4 years for men and women at 35.1 years
My father lived to 90 and my mother to 91.
For me to match what my parents and grandmother achieved,
I would have to live to be 110 years old.
Both of my parents lived what I think of as a bonus life.
Each lost two siblings in infancy,
and both grew up without fathers.
My maternal grandfather died of gastrointestinal disease in his mid-thirties,
While my paternal grandfather defected to North Korea following his oldest son.
They stayed in touch with life itself — grounded, steady, and unshaken by the small troubles that came their way.
Twenty years and three months and Eighteen years and three months.
That was my father’s and mother’s age when the Korean War started seventy five years ago.
Both suddenly became the de facto heads of their households, filling the void left by missing fathers.
My father faced death numerous times during the war and was captured by the Korean People’s Army (조선인민군) – three times.
My mother’s family escaped the war zone by chartered boat, navigating around battle areas and retreating coalition forces during the 1.4 후퇴 – The Retreat of January 4th, 19511
After surviving the war, both of my parents must have felt that a second life had been granted to them.
“That which does not kill us makes us stronger”
“He who has a why to live can bear almost any how”
Unlike my grandparents’ and parents’ generation, my own has lived with dramatically reduced infant mortality and greatly improved living conditions.
And yet, it seems that my parents were the stronger ones.
They had a clearer reason for existence — a why that anchored them through loss, war, and rebuilding. They understood, perhaps better than we do, what life required of them. As Viktor Frankl observed, strength arises not merely from endurance, but from purpose.
While my parents’ generation endured deprivation and war, mine was born into recovery and growth.
We inherited stability
Where their survival demanded cooperation, endurance, and gratitude for the smallest victories,
Ours often revolves around choice, comfort, and self-expression.
Theirs was a world of scarcity that revealed character. Ours is a world of abundance that often obscures it.
When my parents spoke of hardship, it was rarely in bitterness.
They told their stories without embellishment, as if suffering were simply part of the landscape of being alive.
To them, life was not something to be optimized — it was something to be upheld.
Each day was a continuation of a second chance.
Now, as I enter the later chapters of my own life,
I see more clearly what that “bonus life” truly meant. It was not about longevity, but about presence — a quiet persistence that came from knowing what could have been lost.
My parents never sought meaning in abstract ideals; they found it in duty, in family, in rebuilding what was broken.
And perhaps that is the lesson for those of us who live in safer times — that a full life is not measured by how much we gain, but by how deeply we remain faithful to what life asks of us.

Recent visit to a large, modern, metropolitan area confirmed a theory.
A suspicion that has been building and partially tested over the years.
I have become a country mouse than a city mouse.
All of the modern conveniences were present.
Clean, well organized streets with buses and subways that served virtually all parts of the city.
Law abiding citizens, adding to the sense of well being and safety.
Modern office and apartment buildings that housed hundreds if not thousand persons in a single edifice.
Places that will satisfy basics as well as un-stated needs in an instant.
In fact, the only thing missing were more customers that will consume all of the material goods that were readily available in this metropolitan area and beyond.
There were few things that I needed coaching up to become more like the citizen of this city.
Like navigating the maze of the underground transportation system. Calling taxis using the new peer to peer network. Ordering food through installed kiosks at each table.
In time, I would become more proficient and could mimic being a local person.
However, there was one trend that proved to be difficult to overlook.
Tasks in big city were mostly transactional.
No room, or more accurately no time for getting personal or have a human interaction.
In an area, covered with as if 人山人海, I felt alone. Tides of people in the morning and even more people in the evening hours.
I would not know how to adjust to this setting where people appear to congregate and get things done, then retire to their areas of refuge, into their cubicles in the sky.
I could adjust, but given a choice, I will take a small town with its inconveniences over a big town living.
